items.answer: Vuforia is a cross-platform augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) that uses computer vision to recognize and track images and objects in the real world for creating AR applications.

Unity is a popular cross-platform game engine and developer environment that provides an editor interface and implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, enabling developers to create, build, and deploy 2D and 3D interactive content, including XR experiences.
A trigger is a Unity collider configured using the isTrigger property that does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.

A collider is a component in a physics engine that defines a game object's shape for physical collisions. It can be static, use primitive or mesh shapes, or be a trigger that other colliders pass through.

Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.
A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.

questions.question: Why does a programmer write C# scripts for a customized experience in Unity?
options: To change the built-in support
To create a new type of game object
To compile scripts in an integrated development environment
To install the scripting environment
questions.explanation: Unity's built-in support provides only the behavior that the environment already has, so scripts are written to change that behavior for a customized experience. Installing the environment or compiling scripts are setup steps, not the reason for writing a script.

questions.question: What kind of Unity entity is a newly created C# script?
options: A new type of game object in Unity
A new type of project folder in Unity
A new type of component in Unity
A new type of prefab in Unity
questions.explanation: A Unity C# script is essentially a new component type that can be attached to a game object to control its behavior. It is not itself a game object, prefab, or folder.

questions.question: What can a C# script component do after it is attached to a game object in Unity?
options: It can create a new C# script and open it in an IDE while the game runs in Unity
It can replace the built-in support and generate game objects while the game runs in Unity
It can install the scripting environment and compile scripts while the game runs in Unity
It can trigger events and modify component properties while the game runs in Unity
questions.explanation: Once attached, the script works when the game is executed and lets the developer trigger events, change component properties over time, and respond to input. It does not perform environment setup, create the script itself, or replace the built-in support.

questions.question: How are C# scripts usually created in Unity compared with most other assets?
options: Outside Unity through a separate compiler in Unity
In Visual Studio before the Unity project starts in Unity
In the Inspector after a game object is selected in Unity
Directly in Unity through the IDE interface in Unity
questions.explanation: C# scripts are usually created directly within Unity using the interface provided by the IDE. The other options describe separate tools, wrong timing, or a wrong place in the Unity interface.

data.text: Unity's built-in support provides a usable experience, but it only gives what the system supplies, so customized XR applications require programmer-written scripts. Unity sets up a C# scripting environment automatically, with IDE support such as Visual Studio, so scripts can be written in C#. A script is created in Unity and attached to a game object as a component, then runs while the game executes to control objects, trigger events, and respond to input.
points: Unity's built-in support gives only the base experience; customized XR experiences need programmer-written scripts.
Unity's scripting environment is installed automatically and supports IDEs; Visual Studio is default on Windows and Mac.
Unity scripts use C#, an object-oriented programming language created by Microsoft.
An attached Unity C# script component controls a game object while the game executes, triggering events and responding to input.
Unity C# scripts are usually created inside Unity via Assets, Create, C# Script in the selected project folder.

questions.question: In a Unity C# script, what does the public class name usually match?
options: The project folder name
The active scene name
The script file name
The attached game object name
questions.explanation: A Unity C# script normally defines a public class whose name matches the script file name.

questions.question: Which statement describes when a Unity Update function runs?
options: It is called in each frame while the script executes
It is called when a game object is attached to the scene
It is called once when the script is first started
It is called when a new C# script is created
questions.explanation: Update is the Unity function that runs each frame while the script is active, while Start is the starting-point function.

questions.question: In a Unity script, how does Vector3 represent the position of a 3D point?
options: It stores an orientation as vector elements
It stores three coordinates as vector elements
It stores a pose as vector elements
It stores two coordinates as vector elements
questions.explanation: Vector3 represents a 3D point by storing its three coordinates as the three elements of a vector.

questions.question: In Unity, where would a developer look for a script variable's value and for a Debug.Log message?
options: Variable value in the Inspector, message in the console output
Variable value in the console output, message in the Inspector
Variable value in the Inspector, message in the script asset
Variable value in the script asset, message in the console output
questions.explanation: Variable values can be checked in the Inspector, while Debug.Log sends its message to the console output after execution.

data.text: The basic Unity C# script structure defines where code is placed: a namespace, using statements, and a public class, usually inheriting MonoBehaviour, named after the file. Start and Update then provide the script's starting point and per-frame execution, while Vector3 represents a 3D point by three coordinates. Once the script has run, a developer can inspect variable values in the Inspector and read Debug.Log messages in the console.
points: A Unity C# script has a namespace, using statements, and a public class, usually inheriting MonoBehaviour, named after the file.
A Unity script has Start called as its starting point and Update called in each frame during execution.
In Unity scripts, the Vector3 data type stores three coordinates to represent a 3D point's position.
In Unity, double-clicking a script asset opens its code, and the Inspector in the Unity Hub editor shows variable values.
Debug.Log in a Unity script prints a message to the console output after the script runs.

questions.question: What is the result of calling Destroy(gameObject, 5f) in Unity?
options: the game object is created again in the scene after five seconds
the script is no longer running in the scene after five seconds
the scene is paused in the editor after five seconds
the game object is no longer in the scene after five seconds
questions.explanation: In Unity, Destroy with a delay removes the game object from the scene after the specified number of seconds. A delay of 5f means the object disappears five seconds after the call.

questions.question: In a Unity script, why does a programmer usually define user-defined functions?
options: to provide behavior that the scene selects at runtime
to provide behavior that the programmer specifies
to provide behavior that the hardware supplies for the user
to provide behavior that Unity supplies for the script
questions.explanation: User-defined functions are written by the programmer to add behavior that Unity does not already supply. Prebuilt functions are the ones Unity provides for script operation.

questions.question: What happens when a gameplay event activates a Unity event function?
options: Unity passes control to the function, executes its body, and leaves control with the function
Unity passes control to the function, executes its body, and returns control to the scene
Unity passes control to the function, executes its body, and returns control to Unity
Unity passes control to the function, skips its body, and returns control to Unity
questions.explanation: A Unity event function is activated by an event during gameplay: Unity gives it control, the function body runs, and control is passed back to Unity. The function body is not skipped, and control is not kept by the function.

questions.question: How can Unity event functions be used to impose realistic behavior?
options: interactive behavior in update functions and physical behavior in initialization functions
interactive behavior in physics-event functions and physical behavior in GUI event functions
physical behavior in GUI event functions and interactive behavior in update functions
physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in GUI event functions
questions.explanation: Unity event functions can impose realistic behavior by putting physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in GUI event functions. Reversing or mixing those roles does not match how those event functions are used.

questions.question: What do Unity's OnCollision event functions relate to?
options: a script being called as the starting point
contact being made or broken
a game object disappearing after a delay
a collider being configured as a trigger
questions.explanation: OnCollision event functions relate to contact being made or broken. A collider configured as a trigger is associated with OnTrigger-type functions, not OnCollision functions.

data.text: Unity scripts use prebuilt functions, such as MonoBehaviour's Destroy function, and user-defined functions to control game objects. Event functions are Unity functions activated by gameplay events, including update, initialization, graphical user interface, collision, and trigger events. These event functions can impose realistic physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in graphical user interface event functions.
points: Unity's MonoBehaviour Destroy function destroys a game object from the scene after a delay specified in seconds.
Unity scripts use prebuilt functions and user-defined functions, with user-defined functions typically part of a good script.
Unity event functions are activated by gameplay events, including update, initialization, graphical user interface, collision, and trigger functions.
Unity event functions can impose realistic physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in GUI event functions.

activities.title: Order the events in Unity event-function activation

items.title: Order the events in Unity event-function activation
steps: Unity passes control to the event function

questions.question: What is the effect of dragging a prefab into the My Prefab field of a script component?
options: It gives the script a reference to the prefab for runtime instantiation
It gives the prefab a reference to the script for runtime instantiation
It gives the scene a reference to the prefab for runtime instantiation
It gives the inspector window a reference to the prefab for runtime instantiation
questions.explanation: The My Prefab field stores a reference in the script so the script can instantiate that prefab at runtime. Dragging the prefab there does not create a scene instance, reverse the reference, or put the reference in the scene or inspector as the operating object.

questions.question: What distinguishes a do-while loop from a for or while loop?
options: The condition is checked before the body executes
The condition is checked until the body executes
The condition is checked after the body executes
The condition is checked while the body executes
questions.explanation: A do-while loop is exit-controlled: the body runs first and the condition is checked afterward, so the body executes at least once. A for or while loop is entry-controlled, checking the condition before the body can run.

questions.question: What is a suitable use for a foreach loop?
options: Working with a polymorphic collection
Working with a heterogeneous collection
Working with a homogeneous collection
Working with a mixed-type collection
questions.explanation: A foreach loop is suited to arrays or collections of homogeneous data types because it lets the programmer work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types. Non-homogeneous or mixed-type collections are not the described use case.

data.text: A script can instantiate a prefab at runtime and use conditionals and loops to control behavior. Giving the script a reference to a prefab comes first, then execution can be directed. Conditional if-else statements choose between branches, while for, while, do-while, and foreach provide different ways to repeat work.
points: To instantiate a prefab at runtime, attach it to the script component's My Prefab field in the editor.
The scripting environment supports standard conditional if-else statements.
For and while are entry-controlled loops, and do-while is exit-controlled, running at least once before checking.
A foreach loop handles homogeneous arrays or collections directly, without dealing with individual data types.

questions.question: What does the Transform property on a game object store?
options: Its collider, renderer, and rigidbody
Its position, rotation, and scale
Its name, tag, and layer
Its material, texture, and opacity
questions.explanation: A game object's Transform holds its position, rotation, and scale, and those values can be changed from a script.

questions.question: How does a Unity coroutine continue after it pauses?
options: It starts the method again from the beginning on the following frame
It waits for a user event before it can resume the method
It resumes where the method left off on the following frame
It waits for a scene change before it can resume the method
questions.explanation: A coroutine pauses, gives control back to Unity, and later continues from the same point on the following frame rather than restarting or waiting for another event.

questions.question: Why are Unity coroutines not treated as ordinary threads?
options: They run on separate threads and do not block other scripts
They run in separate processes and finish while the game is loading
They run on the main thread and do not spawn individual threads
They run on worker threads and share work with the hardware
questions.explanation: Coroutines are not threads: even when they pause and resume, their work still happens on the main thread and they do not create separate threads.

questions.question: What makes a gradual opacity fade visible in Unity?
options: Changing the shader so Unity can skip rendering intermediate frames
Waiting for a scene change so Unity can start the fade at a stable frame
Setting the opacity once so Unity stores the final material
Lowering the opacity over several frames so Unity renders intermediate values
questions.explanation: A fade is visible only when the opacity changes over a sequence of frames, allowing Unity to render the intermediate values; a one-time change is not perceived as a gradual fade.

questions.question: In InvokeRepeating, what do the two time values specify?
options: The initial delay and the repeat interval, in seconds
The minimum interval and the maximum interval, in seconds
The pause length and the method's run time, in seconds
The start time and the end time, in seconds
questions.explanation: InvokeRepeating takes the first time as the delay before the method starts and the second time as the interval between repeated calls, both measured in seconds.

data.text: Unity scripts can change a game object's transform property to control its position, rotation, and scale. Coroutines pause and resume a method across frames, and they do not create separate threads; this frame-by-frame control is needed to show a gradual opacity fade over several frames. InvokeRepeating supplies timed repetition by calling a named method after an initial delay and then repeatedly at an interval.
points: A Unity object's transform property stores position, rotation, and scale, and scripts can change it to control behavior.
A Unity coroutine spreads a task across frames by pausing execution, returning control to Unity, and resuming.
Unity coroutines are not threads, and their synchronous operations still execute on the main thread.
A gradual opacity fade must be defined as a coroutine and started so its opacity changes over several visible frames.
InvokeRepeating calls a named method after an initial delay and repeats it at an interval, both in seconds.

questions.question: When a Unity project uses an input device beyond the mouse, keyboard, and buttons, what role does imported SDK input support play?
options: A requirement for the mouse, keyboard, and buttons
A replacement for Unity's inbuilt input support
An extension of Unity's inbuilt input support
A setting that starts the build process
questions.explanation: For device-specific inputs not covered by Unity's inbuilt handling, imported SDK input support can be used to extend that support. It does not replace the built-in handling for mouse, keyboard, and buttons, nor does it start the build.

questions.question: After a script is written and a Unity system is built, what is the last stage in the Unity development environment?
options: Editing the scripts for the scenes
Importing SDK input support
Publishing or deploying the system
Rebuilding the system again
questions.explanation: Once the script is written and the system is built, the final stage is to publish or deploy it. Importing SDK support, rebuilding, or editing scripts are development steps that come before that final publication stage.

questions.question: In the Unity Build Settings window, what does the platform section determine?
options: The start of the build process
The input devices supported by scripts
The deployment target for the system
The scenes included in the build
questions.explanation: The platform section selects the platform to which the system is deployed. The scenes are managed by the Scenes in Build panel, the build is started by the Build or Build and Run button, and input support is handled by scripting and SDK input support.

data.text: Unity's interactive scripting and build deployment work together. Scripting handles built-in mouse, keyboard, and button inputs, while imported SDKs may extend support for device-specific inputs. After the script is written and the system is built, the Build Settings window supports publishing by managing included scenes, selecting the target platform, and starting the build.
points: Unity scripting handles built-in mouse, keyboard, and button inputs; imported SDKs may extend support for device-specific inputs.
Unity's Build Settings window is where publishing happens, managing scenes, platform, and the Build or Build and Run buttons.

questions.question: Why does a developer import a platform-specific SDK into Unity?
options: To use Unity functions that the platform's built-in support lacks
To use platform functions that Unity's built-in support includes
To use platform functions that Unity's built-in support lacks
To use application functions that the platform's built-in support lacks
questions.explanation: Importing an external SDK lets the developer use platform functions that Unity's built-in support does not provide. The reversed options mistake which side supplies the missing functions.

questions.question: In Unity's layered architecture, where is an imported SDK layer placed?
options: Above the application layer in the installed package, with its APIs used by the application
Above the Unity layer in the installed package, with its APIs used by the application
Outside the installed package, as part of the hardware platform, with its APIs used by the application
Below the Unity layer in the installed package, with its APIs used by the application
questions.explanation: The application is the top layer, while the SDK layer sits on top of the Unity layer and is treated as part of the installed Unity package. The application uses the SDK's APIs.

questions.question: Why is Vuforia used in a Unity-based augmented reality project?
options: To provide efficient platform build settings, deployment, and publishing where Unity's built-in support is limited
To provide efficient VR object detection, recognition, and tracking where Unity's built-in support is limited
To provide efficient AR user interaction, navigation, and scene management where Unity's built-in support is limited
To provide efficient AR object detection, recognition, and tracking where Unity's built-in support is limited
questions.explanation: Vuforia is an AR SDK focused on object recognition or computer vision operations such as detection, recognition, and tracking. Unity's built-in support for these operations is not extensive, so an external AR package is needed for seamless and efficient performance.

data.text: External SDKs are imported when a specified hardware platform provides functions that Unity's built-in support does not include. In Unity's layered architecture, the SDK layer sits above Unity and below the application, and its package APIs are used. Vuforia is an AR SDK for object recognition, an area where Unity's built-in support is not extensive or good, so the integration steps are to install Unity Hub, import the SDK, use Unity and SDK functions, then compile, build, and deploy.
points: If a specified hardware platform offers functions not in Unity, the developer imports an SDK or package to use them.
In Unity's layered architecture, the application is top, the SDK layer is above Unity, and its package APIs are used.
Vuforia is an AR SDK primarily for object recognition and computer vision tasks such as detection, recognition, and tracking.
Unity's built-in support for object detection, recognition, and tracking is not extensive or good, so external packages are needed.
The basic steps include installing Unity Hub, importing the SDK, using Unity and SDK functions, compiling, building, and deploying.

activities.title: Order the basic steps of SDK integration in Unity

items.title: Order the basic steps of SDK integration in Unity
steps: The SDK package is imported into the Unity environment
The functions of both Unity and the SDK are used
The system is compiled, built, and deployed

questions.question: What does the Vuforia database package imported into Unity mainly provide?
options: The tracked images needed for recognition
The Android build settings for the device
The license key for the Vuforia account
The 3D model used in the sample
questions.explanation: The database package holds the target images or markers that Vuforia can recognize in the real world. The 3D model, license key, and Android player settings are added to the project through separate steps.

questions.question: In the Unity sample, how does adding the Vuforia SDK extend the built-in environment?
options: It adds recognition of real-world images and objects
It adds markerless placement of virtual objects in the scene
It adds a built-in 3D modeling tool for assets
It adds access to device-specific sensor and input data
questions.explanation: Vuforia extends Unity by supplying image-recognition functionality, i.e., recognizing images and objects in the real world. Access to device-specific sensory or input data is the role of other platform-specific SDKs, not Vuforia.

questions.question: When the Android platform is selected in the sample, what does Build and Run do?
options: It creates a database package and uploads it to the Vuforia website
It creates an APK and installs it on the connected Android device
It creates a scene file and copies it to the Android device
It creates a 3D model and assigns it to the image target
questions.explanation: Build and Run packages the Unity project as an Android APK and deploys it to the connected device. It does not generate the marker database, the 3D model, or a standalone scene file.

questions.question: What triggers the operations in an image target behavior script?
options: Connection of the Android device over USB
Recognition of the marker by the Vuforia engine
Selection of the image target in the Unity editor
Assignment of the 3D model in the inspector
questions.explanation: The behavior script runs after the Vuforia engine recognizes the marker. Editor selection, device connection, and model assignment are setup actions that do not trigger the script.

data.text: Vuforia, a licensed cross-platform augmented reality SDK, is used to extend Unity with image recognition. After adding the Vuforia SDK, account license, and target database, the sample scene is configured with an image target, a 3D model, and a behavior script. For Android, application-specific player settings are set, the APK is built and run, and recognizing the marker image displays the 3D model over it.
points: Vuforia is a cross-platform augmented reality SDK that requires a license.
Setting up Vuforia in Unity requires adding the SDK, its license, and a target database.
The sample scene assigns a marker image and 3D model to Vuforia's image target, and a script acts after recognition.
For Android, application-specific Unity player settings are set, then the APK is built and run to the device.
In the running app, recognizing the matching marker image displays the 3D model in place of it.

questions.question: What allows a basic virtual or augmented reality system to be built with less programming than a customized one?
options: Hand-written code support for basic functions
Menu-based IDE support for basic functions
Imported SDK support for basic functions
Custom scripting support for basic functions
questions.explanation: A basic system can be assembled with menu-based IDE support without scripting, while a customized experience requires scripting and therefore more programming. SDKs are not the reason a basic system needs less code.

questions.question: In an XR project, importing a software development kit is mainly needed for ?
options: Functionality that exceeds the support of the Unity development environment
Functionality that matches the support of the Unity development environment
Functionality that is already included in the support of the Unity development environment
Functionality that can be created with the support of the Unity development environment
questions.explanation: SDKs are imported when the required functions go beyond what the Unity environment already provides. If the functionality is already available or can be created inside the environment, an SDK is not the main reason for importing one.

questions.question: What do the Programmer's and Developer's Manuals mainly provide for XR development?
options: Further details on building and deploying XR systems and writing code
Device-specific support for building and deploying XR systems and writing code
A customized experience for building and deploying XR systems and writing code
Menu-based IDE support for building and deploying XR systems and writing code
questions.explanation: The manuals are sources of further details about building, deploying, and coding XR systems. They do not themselves provide device-specific support, menu-based IDE support, or a customized experience.

data.text: Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems is primarily programming work. The required amount of scripting varies with functionality, from menu-based basic systems to customized scripted experiences, while device-specific SDKs are imported when Unity development environment support is exceeded. The Programmer's Manual and Developer's Manual provide further details for building, deploying, and writing code.
points: Building XR systems is mainly programming: basic systems can use menu-based IDE support, while customized experiences need scripting.
SDKs provide device-specific support for XR systems and are imported when required functionality exceeds Unity development environment support.
The Programmer's Manual and Developer's Manual on the respective websites give further details on building, deploying, and writing XR code.

questions.question: Why is scripting needed for a customized Unity experience even though menu-based integrated development environment support can build a basic system?
questions.reference_answer: Menu-based IDE support can build a basic system without scripting, but Unity's built-in support provides only the experience the system already provides. A C# script attached as a component to a game object gives the developer a component that behaves as desired rather than according to the built-in support, so a customized experience requires writing such scripts.

questions.question: Why must a gradual opacity fade in Unity be implemented as a coroutine rather than as a function called once?
questions.reference_answer: A gradual opacity fade is visible only when the opacity value is reduced over a sequence of frames so Unity renders the intermediate values. A coroutine can pause execution, return control to Unity, and continue on the following frame, so the change can be spread frame by frame. A function called once cannot produce that visible fade.

questions.question: Why does the marker-based augmented reality sample use Vuforia instead of relying only on Unity's built-in support?
questions.reference_answer: Unity's built-in support for object recognition, computer vision, object detection, and tracking is not extensive or very good. Vuforia is an augmented reality software development kit primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking. Its setup requires a database containing the marker images, so the Vuforia engine can recognize the marker and display the three-dimensional model in place of the marker.
